extracted.intended_audience: readers of Lincoln-Douglas debates; historians, students, and general readers interested in 19th-century political rhetoric
extracted.subtask_description: Transcription and correspondence from the 1858 Lincoln-Douglas Senate campaign debates, containing Lincoln's replies, rhetorical strategies, and argumentative standards. Useful for studying political argument, evidence, and rhetorical norms of the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden to support affirmative charges
rubrics_metrics.description: When a man makes an affirmative charge, he must offer some proof to show the truth of what he says.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln insists that a person making an affirmative allegation has the right and obligation to provide proof; a man cannot simply assert a fact and expect others to accept it. He notes one "cannot prove a negative," but still demands evidence for positive claims. (Original phrasing: "when a man makes an affirmative charge, he must offer some proof to show the truth of what he says.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral rule on asserting unknowns
rubrics_metrics.description: "He who asserts a thing which he does not know to be true falsifies as much as he who knowingly tells a falsehood."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this rule to debate: do not assert as fact what you do not know. The standard treats careless assertions and intentional lies as equally blameworthy in rhetorical morality; speakers should distinguish belief from knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish belief from knowledge and offer evidence for beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: When charging a conspiracy or similar serious matter, state whether you 'know' it or only 'believe' it, and be prepared to produce supporting evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln states he "did not profess to know" the conspiracy but that he believed it and had arranged evidence to support that belief. The guidance: be explicit about the epistemic status of your claims and marshal witnesses/facts when claiming belief that implies wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to correct factual errors when pointed out
rubrics_metrics.description: If evidence presented contains anything false or erroneous, the presenter should accept correction and retract without rancor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln says if any of the evidence he produced "had stated anything which was false or erroneous, it needed but that Judge Douglas should point it out, and I would have taken it back, with all the kindness in the world." Speakers should invite correction and correct mistakes promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show basis for knowledge claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If you claim to 'know' something, you must show how you know it—provide the sources or process that produced that knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln: "if a man says he knows a thing, then he must show how he knows it." This requires transparency about sources, conversations, records, or methods used to reach factual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor arguments in founders' principles and historical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: When interpreting constitutional or political questions, invoke the original basis on which the founders placed institutions and compare contemporary proposals to that standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln appeals to Jefferson, Washington, Madison and the "original basis" of restricting slavery from new territories. Guidance: use historical precedent and founders' practice as a relevant standard to evaluate modern legislative changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete analogy and narrative to show plausibility of a conspiracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ vivid analogies (e.g., the framed timbers illustration) to connect disparate facts and make an inference of preconcert intelligible and persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln's "framed timbers" analogy demonstrates how separate pieces, when fitted together, indicate prior coordination. Use analogies to help audiences see how circumstantial evidence can point to a planned scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define key terms precisely and test logical implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the meaning of contested terms (e.g., 'popular sovereignty') and explore their logical consequences under existing legal rulings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln defines popular sovereignty as applied to slavery and then tests it against the Dred Scott decision's logic. The rubric: don't rely on vague slogans—clarify meanings and follow them through to their consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct misrepresentation by quoting original statements
rubrics_metrics.description: When an opponent misrepresents you, answer by producing your original statements or texts rather than merely denying the misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln reads from his Peoria and Springfield speeches to rebut Douglas's characterization. Guidance: quoting primary texts prevents straw-man summaries and lets the audience judge accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer calm explanation over personal invective
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid escalating to personal attacks (accusing someone of lying); calmly point out errors or alternative explanations instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln criticizes Douglas for rushing to call him a liar and suggests it would be better to "calmly and good-humoredly point out" the real reasons for actions. Rhetorical norm: civility and reasoned exposition are more persuasive and respectable than ad hominem smears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close textual reading of legislation to infer intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the exact wording of bills and statutes (e.g., unusual uses of 'State' in the Nebraska Bill) to detect clues about legislative intent or forthcoming legal developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln points to the odd insertion of 'State' in a territorial bill as suggestive of a larger plan. The guidance: small textual anomalies can be meaningful when reconstructing motive or design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain composure and good humor under attack
rubrics_metrics.description: A speaker should remain good-humored and composed even when flattered or attacked, as a rhetorical and ethical posture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln notes he was softened by Douglas's flattery but remained composed. The practical guidance: composure preserves credibility and focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise in normative claims about equality and rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between equality in 'all respects' and equality in natural rights (life, liberty, pursuit of happiness); state clearly what form of equality is being asserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln clarifies he does not mean social and political equality in all respects but insists on equal entitlement to the natural rights enumerated in the Declaration. The rubric: avoid conflating distinct senses of 'equality' in moral/political argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insist on reciprocal fairness in debate procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: In a point-by-point questioning format, require reciprocity—don't allow one-sided 'catechizing' without opportunity to return questions or have equal time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln refuses to answer a string of questions one after another unless Douglas reciprocates. Debate procedure should be balanced so each party can both question and respond adequately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use official records as direct evidence to rebut factual charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult and cite legislative or voting records to rebut assertions about a speaker's past conduct (e.g., votes on funding soldiers during the Mexican War).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln says an examination of records will show he did vote to supply soldiers similarly to Douglas. The guidance: documentary sources are authoritative rebuttals to alleged inconsistencies or misconduct.
